query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys, the retention of toughness is governed by the distribution of the principal elements at grain boundaries, a process mediated by sluggish diffusion inherent to multicomponent mixing. When elements such as Ni, Cr, and Mn segregate into very fine clusters at the grain boundaries, they reduce local cohesion and promote intergranular cracking. Thus, treatments that encourage a homogeneous elemental distribution (or shift segregation into preexisting secondary phases) will preserve toughness, whereas conditions that promote rapid clustering at grain boundaries will lead to toughness loss.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, coarse‐grained equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEA (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) without engineered secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment or adjust the cooling rate to vary the extent of elemental segregation at the grain boundaries. For example, compare a slow annealing process (to promote segregation) with rapid quenching (to preserve a homogeneous elemental distribution) or use grain boundary segregation engineering that shifts segregation into preformed Cr-rich secondary precipitates.
generation.conditions: Conduct tensile tests at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures under a controlled atmosphere and strain rate to isolate the effects of microstructural changes without complications from oxidation or extrinsic factors.
generation.structural_mediator: Very fine clusters of elements such as Ni, Cr, and Mn concentrated at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Nanosegregation at grain boundaries, influenced by sluggish diffusion from multicomponent mixing, weakens intergranular cohesion and facilitates the initiation and propagation of intergranular cracks, thereby reducing overall toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA samples that experience enhanced grain boundary segregation (via slow annealing) will exhibit lower fracture toughness (e.g., reduced ductility and more intergranular fracture features) compared to baseline samples processed under rapid quenching conditions that maintain a uniform elemental distribution.
generation.baseline: HEA specimens processed via standard protocols (without extended annealing) that exhibit moderate and uniform toughness with minimal grain boundary nanosegregation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single‐phase, coarse‐grained high-entropy alloys where principal elements (such as Ni, Cr, and Mn) are present in similar proportions. It may not hold in multi‐phase systems or in alloys dominated by other toughening mechanisms (e.g., transformation-induced plasticity or extensive deformation twinning).
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence indicates a correlation between GB segregation and ductility loss, the precise quantitative relationship between the degree of nanosegregation and toughness reduction is uncertain, and other extrinsic factors (such as oxidation at high temperatures) might confound the observations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens with identical starting compositions. Subject one set to a slow annealing treatment (expected to promote nanosegregation at grain boundaries) and the other to rapid quenching (expected to maintain a homogeneous distribution). Characterize the grain boundary composition using atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM, then perform tensile tests to quantify fracture toughness and examine fracture surfaces for intergranular versus transgranular failure modes.
measurements: Fracture toughness (fracture initiation toughness, ductility metrics)
Grain boundary chemistry and segregation levels via APT or TEM
Fractography to assess the prevalence of intergranular cracking
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with enhanced grain boundary segregation do not exhibit significantly reduced toughness (or show similar toughness to the homogenized samples) and if fracture surfaces do not reveal an increase in intergranular cracking compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis that nanosegregation governs toughness loss is falsified.

Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.
